title: Investigatio motuum, quibus laminae et virgae elasticae contremiscunt

deep.reconstruction:
This page finishes Lemma 1 (static equilibrium of a planar elastic rod EYF under distributed loads), gives a Scholion generalising it to naturally curved rods, and states Lemma 2 (dynamics).

Setting. Arc length s = EY. Coordinates x(s), y(s) with dx² + dy² = ds². P ds and Q ds are the load components on the element, parallel to the x- and y-axes. Euler takes the bending moment as V/r = V(dy ddx − dx ddy)/ds³, where V is the 'absolute elasticity' (modern EI). Equilibrium of the piece EY gives the moment equation ∫dy∫P ds − ∫dx∫Q ds = V·κ.

Tension (top of this page). The tangential component of the resultant of all forces on EY is N = −(dx/ds)∫P ds − (dy/ds)∫Q ds. This is the tension pulling the element toward E. It is simply the projection of the internal force resultant (−∫P ds, −∫Q ds) onto the tangent.

Scholion §2. If the rod is naturally curved with radius ρ at Y, elasticity acts only insofar as the curvature is increased or decreased. The moment law therefore becomes V(1/r − 1/ρ), i.e. M = EI(κ − κ₀), and the equilibrium equation gains the term −V/ρ. Euler also notes that the integrals ∫P ds, ∫Q ds include any finite forces at the end E. In modern terms these are the boundary conditions on the stress resultants.

Lemma 2 §3. This states the general planar motion problem: find the position and shape of the rod at any time. The next page solves it by d'Alembert's principle. Each load is replaced by P' = P − (S/2g)∂²x/∂t² and Q' = Q − (S/2g)∂²y/∂t². Here S is mass per unit length and 2g is the gravitational acceleration in Euler's units, g being the fall distance in one second. Positions are treated as functions of s and t, with partial derivatives marked by Euler's parentheses. The result is the geometrically exact (large-deflection, inextensible) planar Kirchhoff-rod equations of motion with intrinsic curvature. The paper then specialises to small transverse vibrations.
errors: The sign of the −V/ρ term requires ρ to be signed with the same orientation convention as dy ddx − dx ddy; Euler leaves this implicit.

ideas.what: Tension in the rod obtained as the tangential projection of the resultant of loads on the segment EY
ideas.modern_name: axial force (tangential stress resultant) in a planar inextensible rod
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (1770s works on flexible bodies); systematised by Kirchhoff (1859)
ideas.where_published: Euler's paper on the 'twofold method' (gemina methodus) for equilibrium and motion of flexible bodies, c. 1774–76, Eneström number unsure; this is the 'alio loco' he cites

deep.surprise_reason: The page restates lemmas Euler explicitly says he proved elsewhere: the tension formula, the curvature-change law for naturally curved rods, and d'Alembert's principle for rod motion. All of these are documented by Truesdell in his history of flexible and elastic bodies. Nothing here is new to the record.
